stem:
A 16-year-old is on day 10 of infectious mononucleosis. He now feels well, is afebrile and has no palpable spleen. He is due to play in a rugby grand final in 4 days. His father has paid for an abdominal ultrasound, which reports a spleen of normal size, and asks whether this clears him to play.

What advice is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Play, as the spleen is normal on ultrasound and examination
options.explanation: A normal-sized spleen on a single scan does not make contact sport safe. Splenic rupture is most likely in the first 3 weeks, often in a spleen that cannot be felt, and normal spleen size varies between people.

options.label: B
options.text: Play, wearing padding over the left upper abdomen
options.explanation: Padding does not protect the spleen from the forces of a tackle, and it would encourage a return during the riskiest period.

options.label: C
options.text: No contact sport yet; graded return from about 4 weeks
options.explanation: Correct. Most splenic ruptures in infectious mononucleosis occur in the first 3 weeks, often after minor trauma and in a spleen that cannot be felt. He should avoid contact sport and heavy exertion for now, then return gradually, usually not before about 4 weeks from the start of the illness, once he is well with no enlarged spleen.

options.label: D
options.text: No sport of any kind for 3 months after the illness
options.explanation: Most young people can return to contact sport within about a month. Three months away from all activity is unnecessary.

options.label: E
options.text: Repeat the ultrasound the day before, and play if still normal
options.explanation: A second normal scan adds no safety: on the day of the final he would still be within the period of highest risk.

context: After infectious mononucleosis, avoid contact sport for at least the first 3–4 weeks, even when the spleen cannot be felt or looks normal on ultrasound; the return is graded and clinical.
